fields.expected:
Most of what I've built comes back to retrieval and evaluation. In tSearch, I built a talent-discovery pipeline that starts from seed candidates, expands through public GitHub and Substack collaboration graphs, scores heuristically, and then runs rubric-driven LLM judges over the evidence. The hardest part was not generation, it was retrieval quality and deciding what counted as evidence. I kept discovery and assessment separate so the judges couldn't silently paper over identity-resolution mistakes, and I treated missing evidence as "insufficient evidence" rather than a low score. Working on that made it obvious how much a system like mine is limited by how good the underlying search is.

Separately, my research work has pushed me toward the question of what happens when AI makes generation cheap and judgment scarce. Good search over the whole web is upstream of that. Exa is building the crawling infrastructure, embedding models, and vector retrieval that things like tSearch have to sit on top of, and I'd rather work on that layer than keep building around its limits. I also want to own real pieces of a system, not isolated tickets.

fields.expected:
ClarityAtlas, the iOS health product I lead technically at Open Health Intelligence. I built it end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with Supabase on the backend, and the hardest technical piece was estimating sleep without a wearable. I built a passive sleep-estimation system on HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns, then a "Sleep Twins" matching service that compares users on standardized behavioral features with a weighted distance. The design goal was to help someone see relationships between their own behavior, sleep, and movement instead of staring at isolated metrics.

The part I'm actually proud of is that it got used. We shipped into a live pilot at Hopkins with 30+ users, got into the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps, and received a non-binding indication of about $75,000 for roughly 7 to 8 percent, which we chose not to pursue immediately because we wanted the right long-term partners. Recruiting users, pitching President Daniels after knocking on the doors of Garland Hall, and explaining repeatedly why the thing should exist mattered as much as writing the code.

fields.expected:
I get pulled toward problems where a system has to actually work for someone. With SnapSort I learned that gap the hard way: I built the thing from zero with Flask, AWS, and a multi-model inference pipeline, and getting it to 300+ users taught me that a technically functional system and a product people use are very different. That still drives most of what I do.

The other thing that motivates me is judgment. At Intelehealth I built an evaluation framework comparing AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling, and what stuck with me was how cheap generation is compared to deciding whether an output should be trusted. That question has followed me into my work on the research enterprise, where I've been reading and interviewing people about how institutions select uncertain work, and into how I designed my job-application agent, where free-text and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled.

I also like being wrong in public and updating. Several of my starting theses about research funding did not survive contact with the people I talked to, and rebuilding them is the part I enjoy most.
